label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
output:
**The light from this side**

My last ever night shift finished at half seven on Sunday morning. I drove home down the London Road with the sun coming up in front of me and the shipping forecast on catch‑up, and somewhere around the traffic lights I realised I would never see that particular light from that particular side again. Fourteen years of nights, and that's the bit that got me. Not the last patient, not the last handover. The sky.

I've been trying to write this since Sunday and every version has come out wrong. Either a eulogy or a moan about the NHS, and I don't want to write either of those. I've done my share of moaning and I stand by all of it, but it isn't what this is. This is meant to be an honest account of what nights gave me and what they took, and I'm aware those two lists aren't as separate as they sound.

I started on nights in 2012. I was an SHO then, and I thought I knew what tiredness was. My first winter I sat in the car park at the Infirmary and cried because I could not remember whether I'd given the second dose. I had. I sat there for a while anyway, and I can still picture the frost on the windscreen — a proper frost, the kind you have to scrape. I remember thinking that everyone inside was asleep and it was just me, the frost, and a drug chart in my head. That's the job, a lot of the time. Not the big dramatic stuff. The checking.

People assume nights are about adrenaline. Sometimes they are. Mostly they're about staying kind at five in the morning when you're empty, when you've got nothing left and someone needs a glass of water, or an explanation, or just for you to stand there and not be in a hurry on their behalf. Anyone can be kind at eight in the evening with a full stomach. The night shift is where you find out what your kindness is actually made of.

It's also where the department is most itself. Fewer managers. Fewer meetings. Fewer people watching. What's left is the work and the people doing it, and I've never known honesty or generosity like it. You'll see a nurse who's been on her feet for ten hours sit down with a relative and give them twenty minutes she doesn't have. You'll see a porter appear with a wheelchair before you've finished asking. At four in the morning nobody's job title matters much. I'll miss that more than I can explain to anyone who hasn't worked it.

And at four in the morning, someone makes toast.

I don't know how it started. I've never known. You go into the staff room at four and there's toast. Sometimes there's a lot of toast. Nobody admits to making it. You ask, and everyone looks at you with the flat innocence of people who have been asked before and have their story straight. There's no rota for it, no group chat, no named lead. It simply appears, and it is always exactly what you needed, and there's never quite enough butter and nobody says so.

There was a gentleman last winter, three in the morning, quiet department. He took my hand and told me I had his daughter's hands. I'm not going to give you any more than that. He went home three days later. I don't have anything clever to say about it, and I've thought about it more than I've thought about most of what happened that winter. What I keep coming back to is that I don't remember what I actually did for him. I remember the hand. Maybe that's the whole thing.

Folasade has done nights for twenty‑two years. She's our charge nurse on nights and she still beats me up the stairs, every time, without breathing heavily, which I find personally offensive. She has seen me make every mistake I've ever made and has never once made me feel small about it. When I told her I was going to days she said, "About time," and then she hugged me and told me to look after my knees. That's Folasade.

What it took: my knees, for a start. My sleep, which has been a rumour since about 2015. My blood pressure, which my GP has stopped describing as "a bit high" and started describing as "not a joke any more," in the tone people use when they want you to actually hear them. I'm forty‑two. I'd like to see sixty.

It took things I didn't notice at the time, too. I missed both of my nieces' naming ceremonies. Both of them, over video, from a corridor. My sister lives in Bangalore and she never once complained, not once, and I think about that more than she'd like me to. I've got a family I've mostly loved from a distance, on a screen, at odd hours, because nights are what I could do. That isn't a complaint. It's just true, and I'd rather write it down than pretend otherwise.

So from Monday I'm days only. I'm relieved. I'm also a bit ashamed of being relieved, as though I've handed in a badge I hadn't earned the right to keep. Nights are hard and they're a whole life, and a lot of the people I respect most are still on them, and I am going to be asleep in my own bed at three in the morning while they are not. I don't have a tidy way to feel about that. I've decided I don't need one.

I'll be honest, I don't know what I'll be like on days. I suspect the department at two in the afternoon is a different animal — more people, more paperwork, more voices — and that I'll spend a while learning to be useful in daylight. But I'll be there.

On my last night, at four in the morning, there was toast. I didn't make it. I don't know who did. Folasade was on the stairs, going up two at a time, twenty‑two years in and still beating me. The department was quiet. Someone had put the butter out. And for once I wasn't counting the hours.

I won't be there at four next week. But someone will be. Someone will make the toast. That's the bit I'm holding on to.

---

*Roughly 1,150 words. Easy to trim if you want it shorter — the fridge/car park section and the nieces section are the two that could go without hurting the rest. Happy to adjust the tone anywhere it's drifted too far toward tidy.*
